content.text: Book reference: Chapter 9, pages 287–308. Guided Exercises: Identifying Automatically Started System Processes, Controlling System Services. Lab: Controlling Services and Daemons.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter

systemctl start/stop/enable/disable/status is used constantly, on nearly every task, for the rest of this course and the entire RHCSA exam. Treat this as one of the two or three most important chapters in the book.

systemd is PID 1 — the very first process RHEL 8 starts, and the one that starts everything else: services, mounts, sockets, timers, and the boot process itself. A daemon is simply a background process, conventionally named ending in d (sshd, crond); a systemd "service" often corresponds to one daemon, but can also just mean a one-time action with nothing left running afterward (called oneshot).

systemd's headline features over older init systems: parallel startup of independent services (faster boot), starting daemons on demand rather than always at boot, automatic dependency ordering (a network-dependent service won't even attempt to start before the network is up, avoiding long hung timeouts), and tracking related processes together via Linux control groups (cgroups).
A system service — the type you'll manage most
An IPC socket systemd watches; a connection triggers systemd to start the matching daemon on demand — delays startup cost until the service is actually needed
Watches for a filesystem change (e.g. a new file in a spool directory) and triggers a service in response — common for print queues
A named grouping/synchronization point for other units (e.g. multi-user.target) — the closest systemd equivalent to old-style runlevels
systemctl is THE command for all of this. Unit names and types can be abbreviated in most commands (systemctl status sshd works without typing .service).
Loaded AND active service units (the default view)
Every loaded service unit, active or not
Every INSTALLED unit file and its enablement STATE — including ones never loaded this boot
Full detail: load state, active state, main PID, and recent log lines for one unit
Just active or inactive — script-friendly, one word
failed if it errored during startup, active if fine, unknown/inactive if stopped cleanly
Every service that failed to start — a fast first stop when troubleshooting
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — list-units vs. list-unit-files — know the difference cold

list-units only shows what systemd has actually loaded/attempted this boot — a service that's installed but never triggered won't appear. list-unit-files shows every installed unit and whether it's set to start at boot, regardless of whether it's running right now. Confusing these two is a common way to miss a disabled-but-installed service during troubleshooting.
Whether the unit's config file was found and parsed successfully
Current runtime state — see the state table below
The service's primary process ID and command name
Currently running with one or more live processes
A one-shot action completed successfully; nothing is left running (this is normal, not a failure)
Running, but currently blocked waiting for an event (common for socket-activated units)
Whether it's set to start automatically at the next boot
Can't be enabled directly, but may still be started automatically as a dependency of something that IS enabled
💡 Why this matters — active (exited) is not broken

A oneshot unit that finishes its one-time job and stops is working exactly as designed — active (exited) means success, not failure. Don't confuse this with inactive, which means the unit isn't running at all.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Command reference — the core of this chapter
Every one of these rows is fair game as a direct exam task.
⚠ WARNING — restart changes the PID; reload doesn't — and not every service supports reload

restart is a full stop+start cycle — any in-memory state the process held is gone, and its PID changes. reload asks a running service to re-read its config file in place, keeping the same PID and any live connections. Not every service implements reload — use reload-or-restart when you're not sure, so config changes take effect either way without you needing to check first.
Stop starting at boot (does NOT stop it now)
Start now AND enable at boot, in one line
Stop now AND disable at boot, in one line
⚠ WARNING — start/stop and enable/disable are two completely independent axes

start affects only the current running system; enable affects only future boots. Running systemctl start on its own means the service will vanish again on reboot unless you also enable it — and enable alone won't make anything happen on THIS boot unless you also start it. This is one of the most common RHCSA mistakes: doing only half of the pair when a task actually requires both. --now combines them in one command when you want both.

Mechanically, enable just creates a symbolic link from the unit file (usually under /usr/lib/systemd/system/) into a target's .wants directory (e.g. /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/); disable removes that same link. Nothing about the unit file itself changes either way.
Masking — a harder stop than disable

systemctl mask UNIT links the unit straight to /dev/null, which blocks it from starting at all — manually, at boot, or as a dependency of anything else. systemctl unmask UNIT removes that link and restores normal behavior.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Why masking exists — conflicting services

The book's own example: postfix and sendmail both implement mail delivery and shouldn't both run. Masking the one you're not using prevents it from being accidentally pulled in as a dependency by something else later — disable alone wouldn't stop that indirect activation, mask does.

systemctl list-dependencies UNIT shows everything that unit needs in order to start (add --reverse to instead see what depends ON it). This matters practically: stopping a service doesn't necessarily stop everything associated with it. Stopping cups.service while cups.path and cups.socket are still active means the very next print job silently starts it right back up — you have to stop all three related units to actually keep printing off.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. sudo systemctl status sshd — identify Loaded, Active, and Main PID in the real output.
2. sudo systemctl list-unit-files --type=service | grep enabled | head — see which services are set to survive a reboot on your servera.
3. sudo systemctl stop chronyd; systemctl is-active chronyd (expect inactive); sudo systemctl start chronyd; systemctl is-active chronyd (expect active).

4. sudo systemctl disable chronyd; systemctl is-enabled chronyd (expect disabled) — note the service is likely still running right now, since disable doesn't stop it. sudo systemctl enable chronyd to restore the boot-time setting.
5. sudo systemctl mask chronyd; try sudo systemctl start chronyd — confirm it's refused with "Unit ... is masked." sudo systemctl unmask chronyd to restore normal behavior.
6. systemctl list-dependencies sshd — skim the tree of what sshd needs before it can start.
7. sudo systemctl --failed --type=service — confirm nothing is currently failed on your lab machine.
1. Q1 — You run systemctl enable httpd and walk away, expecting the web server to be reachable immediately. It isn't. Why not, and what single change fixes this going forward?
2. Q2 — systemctl status shows active (exited) for a unit. Is this a failure? What kind of unit typically shows this state?
3. Q3 — Two services on your system both try to manage the same resource and must never run at the same time. disable isn't strong enough here — why, and what command is?
Q1 — enable only sets the service to start at the NEXT boot; it does nothing to the currently running system. Use systemctl enable --now httpd (or run start separately) to have both effects at once.

Q2 — Not a failure — active (exited) means a oneshot unit ran its one-time task successfully and, correctly, has nothing left running afterward. Typically seen on oneshot-type units, not long-running daemons.

Q3 — disable only removes the boot-time symlink but still allows the unit to be started manually or pulled in indirectly as another unit's dependency. systemctl mask links the unit to /dev/null, blocking it from starting under any circumstance — manual, boot, or dependency-triggered — until explicitly unmasked.
systemd (PID 1) manages services, sockets, paths, and targets as units, with parallel startup and automatic dependency ordering.

systemctl status/list-units/list-unit-files/is-active/is-enabled/is-failed are how you inspect current and boot-time state — list-units only shows what's loaded THIS boot, list-unit-files shows every installed unit regardless.

start/stop act on the running system only; enable/disable act on boot-time behavior only — these are independent axes, and forgetting one half of the pair is the single most common mistake in this chapter.
restart changes a service's PID (full stop+start); reload does not (in-place config re-read) — reload-or-restart is the safe default when you're unsure which the service supports.
mask is a strictly harder block than disable — it prevents manual, boot-time, AND dependency-triggered starts, and must be explicitly unmasked to reverse.
